reviews.text: Carey Mulligan isn't one to be left behind, delivering a career-best performance...
reviews.author: Tanzim Pardiwalla

reviews.text: No matter the verdict, it is hard to deny that star and director Bradley Cooper exudes passion for this fearless love story, which is half the battle.
reviews.author: Yasmine Kandil

reviews.text: Maestro is a 129-minute study of the life of an artist, but besides the love story, it doesn’t satisfyingly say much about the artist, his creation or his identity.
reviews.author: Udita Jhunjhunwala

reviews.text: Maestro is a surprisingly pedestrian biopic of a force of nature subject.
reviews.author: Sarah Marrs

reviews.text: Offers little more than something akin to a prolonged high-end fashion mag photoshoot, with a perfunctory script included — until its very end, when it decides to become an actual biopic of Leonard Bernstein.
reviews.author: Milana Vujkov

reviews.text: If you start watching “Maestro” to revel in the unintended camp and over the topness, you can start to have fun. Let the old man go clubbing! Cooper’s voice in the second half and outfits send me over the moon
reviews.author: Sarah Vincent

reviews.text: On a positive note, the performances are excellent.  Cooper channels Bernstein down to his voice patterns.  Mulligan carries most of the emotional baggage of the film and never delivers a false note.
reviews.author: Michael A. Smith

reviews.text: One of 2023's 20 best films.
reviews.author: Matt Brunson

reviews.text: Maestro is fixated on Bernstein’s sexuality—as if it’s the most interesting thing about him.
reviews.author: Brett McCracken

reviews.text: Bernstein exists parallel to her, and Cooper’s performance is daring and convincing, but something doesn’t add up.
reviews.author: A.S. Hamrah

reviews.text: It’s a romance set in our complicated world with our complex feelings and relationships. Even when we find someone with whom we can be our authentic selves, that doesn’t mean we know who our authentic self is.
reviews.author: Rob Dean

reviews.text: It celebrates spontaneity and originality while hitting all the tired Oscar-bait tropes one after the other with numbing sincerity and grim literalness.
reviews.author: Noah Berlatsky

reviews.text: What is undeniable and unambiguous is the music.
reviews.author: Paul Thompson

reviews.text: Maestro has a straight man playing a queer musician, a non-Hispanic woman playing a Latina, and the internet got mad about a NOSE?!
reviews.author: Alicja Johnson

reviews.text: In a singularly compelling performance, Bradley Cooper offers an immersive portrayal ...Easily ranks as one of the finest biopics yet.
reviews.author: Jim Schembri

reviews.text: Cooper delivers a pretentious film. But, I believe, these efforts that are not well rounded become a virtue, since they also contribute to the profile of the character. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Hugo Hernández Valdivia

reviews.text:
Perhaps there's room for a gay #MeToo movement.

Here is a film that needed a serious rewrite, much tighter editing, and direction by a filmmaker other than Bradley Cooper.

At least "Maestro" is an easy movie to forget.
reviews.author: Cole Smithey

reviews.text: An interesting and engrossing film detailing the relationship of Leonard Bernstein and Felicia Montealegere that mostly soars under Bradley Cooper's confident direction, but stumbles with its final few notes. Carey Mulligan delivers career best work here.
reviews.author: John Rocha

reviews.text: Cooper takes himself too seriously and loses sight of the subject in a whirlwind of attention-seeking symphonies.
reviews.author: Eric Marchen

reviews.text: While Bradley Cooper can hold down the technical elements that make Maestro good, his inability to bring the same control to the script does not go unnoticed...
reviews.author: Pallavi Keswani

reviews.text: So wonderful is the performance of Bradley Cooper as composer-conductor Leonard Bernstein.  It is a film well worth seeing for its acting, direction and (not surprisingly) music.
reviews.author: Steve Crum

reviews.text: The film avoids messiness in its timeline, presenting an honest and mature biopic that excels on all fronts.
reviews.author: Filipe Freitas

reviews.text: Despite its limitations, imbalances, and shortcomings, the film maintains the image of Bernstein split between those impulses that dominated him and, in its own way, rescues the figure of Felicia Montealegre, even if as a victim. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Juan José Beteta

reviews.text: This movie is certainly watchable and entertaining, if not compelling. The slow pace of the movie is offset by the fact that it tries to capture the whole spectrum of a complex and supremely accomplished life.
reviews.author: Robert Roten

reviews.text: As memorable as Maestro is as a whole, the sequence that will follow you is one that comes near the end of the film, as Lenny conducts Mahler’s Resurrection at Ely Cathedral....As always in his landmark passion project, Bradley Cooper gets it just right.
reviews.author: Bill Newcott

reviews.text: This is a visually stunning biopic that allows our leads to showcase some phenomenal chemistry. Cooper is excellent, and Mulligan is a scene-stealer. Unfortunately, the film has an identity crisis that keeps it from reaching its true potential
reviews.author: Austin Burke

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper has composed a masterpiece in "Maestro."
reviews.author: Linda Cook

reviews.text: We feel like we’re in good company, everything looks great, the music is excellent, but a fictional drama could have asserted a clear point of view that is lacking here. It’s interesting, but not deeply satisfying.
reviews.author: Abbie Bernstein

reviews.text: Cooper (who co-wrote the film with Josh Singer) realises the futility of simplifying and condensing a person’s legacy into a feature-length film, so he keeps alluding to events that took place in their life between the ‘scenes’ in the film.
reviews.author: Tatsam Mukherjee

reviews.text: Directing a movie is much like conducting an orchestra. Cooper creates the best of both worlds, offering a piece of art that serves as one of the best, most spellbinding movies of the year.
reviews.author: Jonathan Sim

reviews.text: Combines the distilled essence of glittering celebrity with flourishes of showbiz surrealism and, toward the end, a frankly weepy warmth. It's a classic great-man movie.
reviews.author: Kurt Loder

reviews.text: Bernstein’s music is conducted by Yannick Nézet-Séguin. Just hearing the French-Canadian maestro’s renditions through a movie theater’s speakers is worth the price of admission, and Cooper well imitates Bernstein’s rapturous gesticulations on the podium.
reviews.author: Kristian M. Lin

reviews.text: Maestro is a labor of love, and as its director and lead, Cooper has poured himself into it—but at some point all of the effort becomes noticeable, and all of Leonard Bernstein’s magic becomes lost.
reviews.author: Manuela Lazic

reviews.text: Less about the music and perhaps even the man, this film is a stage play with connectivity under the spotlight. Carey Mulligan is a dream floating through time.
reviews.author: Derek Sante

reviews.text: The film itself is a whirlwind, one that lauds the singular beauty of Bernstein’s persona while driving home the truth that befalls anyone in show business: nothing is as important on stage as the folks at home.
reviews.author: Cory Woodroof

reviews.text: Oscar nominations are sure to come for Cooper and Mulligan.
reviews.author: Marie Asner

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper, the director, has a strong conviction that makes his vision arresting cinematically, but Bradley Cooper, the writer, leaves something to be desired.
reviews.author: JD Duran

reviews.text: An intimate, enigmatic love story, provoking more questions than it answers.
reviews.author: Susan Granger

reviews.text: A boring, disjointed biopic that, beyond the performances and some production values that cry out for an Oscar nomination, uselessly repeats the same clichés until it reduces Bernstein's biography to the most absolute indulgence. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Yasser Medina

reviews.text: The director (Bradley Cooper) gets a chance to experiment with more ambitious filmmaking styles.
reviews.author: Korey Coleman

reviews.text: Cooper gives a symphonic performance as legendary American composer and conductor Leonard Bernstein in Maestro and, in his first film as a director since his  2018 update of “A Star Is Born,” is a borderline-masterful conductor himself.
reviews.author: Mark Meszoros

reviews.text: I resent being tear-jerked when the movie’s as lacking in honesty, complexity, and maturity as this one is.
reviews.author: Eileen Jones

reviews.text: Maestro is at once, an audio-visual sniff of vinegar and an experimental head-rush of a biopic.
reviews.author: Prathyush Parasuraman

reviews.text: Despite Cooper and Mulligan's inspired performances, its hesitancy about what story to explore ends up impacting its emotional effectiveness. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Rene Sanchez

reviews.text: Maestro” strives to present Felicia and Lenny as people who love each other, regardless of how unique their relationship is. If you choose, you can appreciate the film solely as being about her side of a love story.
reviews.author: Michael Calleri

reviews.text: If there’s any Oscar-bait note that Maestro misses, it’s not from lack of trying. Bradley Cooper meticulously arranges this film based on the life of acclaimed composer Leonard Bernstein seemingly with the goal of collecting as many awards as possible.
reviews.author: Jeffrey Lyles

reviews.text: It's well worth watching with some dazzling moments, despite not living up to its full potential as the incandescent symphony it could have been.
reviews.author: Brian Bromberger

reviews.text: Mulligan’s display of toughness and fragility is a tour de force. Cooper gives his co-star top billing, but he is the indisputable auteur of this passionate work.
reviews.author: Whang Yee Ling

reviews.text: Maestro is a work that celebrates and admires Berstein. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Sergio Burstein

reviews.text: ...more interested in Cooper as an artist than Bernstein.
reviews.author: Josh Larsen

reviews.text: Cooper manages to express simplicity with wonderful and intoxicating artistic complexity. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Juanma Fernández París

reviews.text: A biopicture about how the marriage of Leonard and Felicia Bernstein influenced his career.
reviews.author: Frederic and Mary Ann Brussat

reviews.text: Carey Mulligan and Bradley Cooper give career defining performances in Maestro, which also features some of the best editing and cinematography of the year.
reviews.author: Lauren Veneziani

reviews.text: A dazzling biopic with terrific lead performances and dynamic direction, though the mysteries of the Bernstein's relationship and the flamboyant conductor-composer's creative life aren't revealed, while his impact on popular culture rates little mention
reviews.author: Jane Freebury

reviews.text: One day, Bradley Cooper will make a truly great film.
reviews.author: Edwin Arnaudin

reviews.text: If you didn't know anything about Leonard Bernstein as composer going into this movie, you'll leave without knowing much more. By trying to balance his story as a composer and his marriage it gave short shrift to both.
reviews.author: Michael Cook

reviews.text: ...a compelling biopic that grows more and more involving as it unfolds...
reviews.author: David Nusair

reviews.text: ‘Maestro’ is no doubt a masterpiece in performance and setting the stage for a story that is far more potent than what we eventually end up seeing on the screen.
reviews.author: Ronak Kotecha

reviews.text: Cooper’s subtle directorial approach smartly allows his actors to do the talking in a glowing biopic that not only basks in nostalgia, it understands it.
reviews.author: Kimberly Pierce

reviews.text: Maestro develops its characters through missing bits, making the film unwhole and underwhelming despite impressive performances and cinematography
reviews.author: Ryan Oquiza

reviews.text: Credit where credit is due - this isn't just a "portrait of a great man" story of tortured genius, but its failure to really pick a lane leaves it feeling oddly incomplete.
reviews.author: Mattie Lucas

reviews.text: I found Maestro intoxicating.
reviews.author: Richard Propes

reviews.text: The sexual focus is but one way of telling the story, but a powerfully revealing one. Instead of seeing Bernstein as a great man or an artistic genius, we take these things for granted and look at the ferment beneath the carapace of fame.
reviews.author: John McDonald

reviews.text: This disingenuous biopic is symptomatic of our era’s convenient reliance on moral equivalency. That’s the only explanation I can think of for Cooper’s peculiar approach to his subject -- half reverential, half reticent.
reviews.author: Armond White

reviews.text: The musical biography “Maestro” is a tour de force for its director and star, Bradley Cooper — which one imagines would suit the person he’s playing, composer and conductor Leonard Bernstein, down to his socks.
reviews.author: Sean P. Means

reviews.text: Perhaps the only surprise here is that we are still surprised by Bradley Cooper.
reviews.author: Sarah Manvel

reviews.text: Puts on a big show but it’s ultimately a hollow vehicle that doesn’t really have anything to say about music, its subjects, love, or sexuality.
reviews.author: Felix Vasquez Jr.

reviews.text: Here it is, folks. The year’s best film.
reviews.author: Robert W. Butler

reviews.text: This is the biggest problem with Maestro: it flattens the man, reduces him to his desires.
reviews.author: Sonny Bunch

reviews.text: If this kind of acting is a little out of fashion—except at the Oscars, obviously—it really works here. The Bernsteins are buzzy and social, jazzed on New York's theatre world, finishing each other's sentences in the film's overlapping dialogue.
reviews.author: Robert Horton

reviews.text: Where Cooper leaves the audience wanting is in his depiction of Bernstein’s life as snippets that are laid out like a colorful patchwork quilt. What the audience would appreciate is more of a story, rather than ... a well produced documentary.
reviews.author: Rick Romancito

reviews.text: In the first five minutes it became apparent that this would not be your typical, candy coated musician biopic, but something much more expansive, compelling and consuming. A masterpiece befitting the master.
reviews.author: Lisa Johnson Mandell

reviews.text: It´s not like the movie needed to be hostile to Bernstein´s legacy or strive to portray him negatively, but by softening the most problematic aspects of his trajectory it comes close to seeming like an institutional affair. [Full review in Portuguese]
reviews.author: Pablo Villaça

reviews.text: To say that Carey Mulligan shines in the film is an understatement; through her outstanding performance, we learn so much about this famous, important person.
reviews.author: Sarah Knight Adamson

reviews.text: [Bradley Cooper's] mimicry eventually becomes overbearing. If an actor is working so hard that all the audience can focus on is the work, rather than the character, it’s self-defeating.
reviews.author: Kyle Smith

reviews.text: Cooper is a warm, generous actor; it shines through in his portrayal of a man who was bursting with vitality, who was eager to please everyone around him -- even when it came at the expense of loving himself.
reviews.author: Luke Goodsell

reviews.text: As director and lead actor, Cooper demonstrated his dual-duty skills admirably in his 2018 remake of A Star Is Born. In Maestro, he takes it to another level in a film that crackles with inventive energy.
reviews.author: Jason Blake

reviews.text: Carey Mulligan is fantastic in this, she glimmers
reviews.author: Stephen A. Russell

reviews.text: It’s as ambitious as Bernstein himself, filled with magnificent flourishes and deep wells of emotion.
reviews.author: Christopher Llewellyn Reed

reviews.text: Maestro is an award-worthy masterpiece of cinema that you should invest your time and energy in. It’s a film about love, romance, and a relationship with a woman and with music.
reviews.author: Romey Norton

reviews.text: Is the movie art, or not? I say yes. Cooper sure seems to be insistent on that interpretation, but his try-hard directorial overtures aren’t a dealbreaker; there’s plenty to appreciate on multiple storytelling levels here.
reviews.author: John Serba

reviews.text: Maestro comes alive as Cooper, who also co-wrote the screenplay, filters Bernstein's passion for life and all its grand indulgences into an intensely physical performance, which peaks in a sweat-drenched conducting sequence that bursts off the screen.
reviews.author: Adam Graham

reviews.text: Maestro is a surprisingly subtle relationship drama even as it captures the over-the-top ebullience of the great conductor.
reviews.author: Margot Harrison

reviews.text: Unsurprisingly, Cooper gives himself and his fellow actors plenty of room to showcase their talents. But while Cooper is impressive as the deeply-flawed yet undeniably gifted and inspiring Bernstein, it’s Mulligan who really shines.
reviews.author: Gregory Wakeman

reviews.text: Though never anything less than ambitious, this is a film in which the parts are greater than the whole, and viewers are apt to feel a little melancholy when they see footage of the real Bernstein.
reviews.author: Nate Bell

reviews.text: Every frame of the film is lovingly crafted with elegance and vintage style.
reviews.author: Gena Radcliffe

reviews.text: The movie’s general lack of candor matches its scrupulous avoidance of controversy and complexity, which does no justice to the complex and controversial characters at the center of the film.
reviews.author: Richard Brody

reviews.text: A captivating drama that’s big, bold and intimate all at once.
reviews.author: Rafer Guzman

reviews.text: The Cooper/Singer screenplay simply trades the clichés of the biopic for the equally trite clichés of the troubled marriage drama.
reviews.author: Daniel M. Kimmel

reviews.text: ‘...a labour of love for Cooper and it sings; the film brings Bernstein and his work to life for a generation who might never have known him, and it’s a striking, waspish, awards-friendly tribute to a remarkable gifted man with talent to burn….’
reviews.author: Eddie Harrison

reviews.text: In Maestro there's visual wonder. In Mulligan's performance there's life. By balancing both, there are glimpses of greatness.
reviews.author: Mireia Mullor

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper disappears into his role and Carey Mulligan devastates with her raw, unyielding performance. Some scenes are gripping, the narrative fails to provide a meaningful connection with the subjects leading to a presentation lacking memorability.
reviews.author: Chris Joyce

reviews.text: There's a sense of fluidity and lyricism to the production that captures the spirit of Bernstein, helping "Maestro" to overcome the limitations of the genre, which often traps viewers in a play-by-play recreation of its subject's life.
reviews.author: Audrey Fox

reviews.text: A pretentious, clichéd, overly dramatic, and flimsy biopic that’s a textbook case of a filmmaker who is more in love with himself than his subject. Cooper thinks he’s making his masterpiece, but nobody appears willing to tell him that indeed he is not.
reviews.author: Louisa Moore

reviews.text: For the 3 minutes of virtuoso physical acting where Bradley Cooper channels Leonard Bernstein's conducting, Mr. Cooper deserves an Oscar. Otherwise "Maestro" brings to mind author Tom Wolfe's description of Bernstein's persona in "Radical Chic": Boring.
reviews.author: Mark Jackson

reviews.text: ... It is incomprehensible that this movie is interpreted as a tribute worthy of the name Maestro. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Gustavo Herrera Taboada

reviews.text: Cooper has clearly been a student of his craft — learning, observing and delivering. A passionate filmmaker and actor, Cooper acts and directs like the maestro he emulates.
reviews.author: Marriska Fernandes

reviews.text: Maestro feels clinical in its exploration of Lenny’s sexuality and Cooper, both as a director and performer, comes across as flashy, but ultimately timid.
reviews.author: Maria Lattila

reviews.text: Bernstein's paradoxes, and the brilliant, often unorthodox ways that Cooper brings them to the screen, make “Maestro” much more fascinating than your typical biopic.
reviews.author: Rob Thomas

reviews.text: Scenes have the snap, crackle and pop of an old-school movie, as if you were watching Cary Grant and Rosalind Russell or Clark Gable and Claudette Colbert.
reviews.author: Wenlei Ma

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper’s work as a director alone is noteworthy, and that is on top of giving one of the best performances of the year as Leonard Bernstein aging him from his 20s to his late sixties.
reviews.author: Paul McGuire Grimes

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper's direction was very ambitious and resulted in beautiful scenes. Carey Mulligan's performance is both powerful and breathtaking, and she truly shines in the movie. Unfortunately, I struggled to have much of any connections to this story.
reviews.author: Elliott Collins

reviews.text: What can you say about such a man in 129 minutes?... Glossy entertainment with bittersweet swerves and of venturesome form.
reviews.author: Ray Pride

reviews.text: There are moments in “Maestro” that are as stunning and bravura as the works of the brilliant man who is the subject of the film.
reviews.author: Nell Minow

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper’s telling of Leonard Bernstein’s life story (warts and all) contains moments of cinematic passion and poetry that make the whole thing worth seeing, even if specific choices create an underlying sense of frustration.
reviews.author: James Berardinelli

reviews.text: MAESTRO is a fascinating, gorgeously shot project, less about the genius artist than it is a playboy in a complicated marriage. Has only one standout musical number, which sadly left me wanting more.
reviews.author: Aaron White

reviews.text: It may not be the most complete portrayal. But it’s a solid enough introduction to a man as layered as his musical compositions.
reviews.author: Keith Garlington

reviews.text: Cooper's second film offers a discordant narrative—a blend of compelling moments with flat notes—so the answer to the question? The movie is made for Mulligan to shine in an otherwise-dull film.
reviews.author: Maxwell Rabb

reviews.text: This is a film you’ll think about long after the credits roll.
reviews.author: Stephen Romei

reviews.text: The film is ambitious and stunning in its visual and emotional story­telling.
reviews.author: Loren King

reviews.text: This film celebrates Leonard Bernstein with an intimate, warm and happy portrait of talent.  [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Aglaia Berlutti

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper directs all elements of this film into a symphony of entertainment.
reviews.author: Jackie K. Cooper

reviews.text: A symphony of love and art... [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Ricardo Gallegos

reviews.text: It's a fascinating story.
reviews.author: tt stern-enzi

reviews.text: In this Leonard Bernstein biopic, Cooper directs, writes, produces and plays the lead. He goes out of his way to honour the celebrated conductor and composer, but forgets a key element: make the subject interesting.
reviews.author: Jorge Ignacio Castillo

reviews.text: Cooper went full “grad student doing his research paper” mode on the figure and delivered a sublime performance as Bernstein.
reviews.author: Rendy Jones

reviews.text: [Cooper's] directorial reserve balances the extravagant acting superbly.
reviews.author: M.V. Moorhead

reviews.text: Maestro is not a complete portrait of Bernstein -- how could it be? The man lived an uncommonly full and rich life. But it is a beautifully mounted, exquisitely acted film that draws us into Bernstein’s world through this intriguing love story.
reviews.author: Max Weiss

reviews.text: The script isn’t bad so much as wrong, from beginning to end, barely giving a sense of why Bernstein was such an iconic figure on the American cultural landscape, and focusing on some of the blandest and least interesting aspects of his life.
reviews.author: Hannah Brown

reviews.text: Maestro might be a big, glossy biopic that – on the surface, at least – sometimes falls into familiar tropes, but it’s worldly and wise enough to get that right, which is enough to elevate it above at least 90 percent of other films in its genre.
reviews.author: John Paul King

reviews.text: It’s a bit much, a performance too far basking in the false glory of a self-generated ovation.
reviews.author: Alistair Harkness

reviews.text: [A] pretentious yet poorly accomplished biopic... [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Carlos Boyero

reviews.text: This, along with a third act that drifts into another kind of cliché-riddled drama with multiple Oscar baits, plagues a movie with some light with shadows. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Pedro Gallego

reviews.text: Maestro might not be the knockout that A Star Is Born is—it’s hard to beat the pipes of Lady Gaga—but it’s arguably more exciting as a directorial effort.
reviews.author: Pat Mullen

reviews.text: It’s a complex and ambitious film, and at times overwhelming, but never less than captivating as multiple sides of the man are explored with visual tenacity.
reviews.author: Victoria Luxford

reviews.text: Stunningly beautiful and immersive, Cooper ups his game as a filmmaker while Mulligan is the clear acting MVP. A towering achievement that's done with utmost love and admiration for the late music virtuoso.
reviews.author: Ruth Maramis

reviews.text: … will be fondly remembered for decades to come.
reviews.author: Robert D’Ottavi

reviews.text: A visionary force of a film with some of the most daring directorial choices you'll see this year, but for all of its creative flourishes, the film loses sight of sharing the story of how Bernstein’s music was created.
reviews.author: Jason Fraley

reviews.text: As a piece of biographical cinema it hits all the right notes harmoniously, despite having an incomplete partiture. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Nestor Bentancor

reviews.text: Right now, Mulligan deserves a Best Actress Oscar, and bravissimo to more nominations all around.
reviews.author: John Urbancich

reviews.text: “Maestro” skims the surface in some respects, but it’s an impressive production, nonetheless.
reviews.author: Russ Simmons

reviews.text: Everything emanates from Cooper’s virtuoso performance or rather his successive performances, first as the eager, brilliant, slightly manic young Bernstein, then as the more formal but still mercurial older man.
reviews.author: Jake Wilson

reviews.text: Above all, Maestro is a love story or rather, the reunion of the love of a conformed couple who knew how to navigate fame and pain from restraint and affection. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Emiliano Basile

reviews.text: At their career-best are Bradley Cooper and Carey Mulligan who eloquently capture the passion of two people experiencing the highs and lows of an artistic life in the spotlight. They’re terrific together
reviews.author: Lynn Venhaus

reviews.text: What Cooper and Mulligan are doing here is extraordinary, delivering exquisitely stylized performances, as big as the screen they’re projected on.
reviews.author: Kimberley Jones

reviews.text: Even for as good as Cooper is, one wonders if the actor should’ve let someone else, perhaps one of his producers Martin Scorsese or Steven Spielberg, helm the picture instead.
reviews.author: Nate Adams

reviews.text: As Bernstein, Cooper gives us a marvelous performance. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Marcelo Stiletano

reviews.text: Yes, Cooper ebulliently re-creates the 1973 performance of Mahler’s Symphony No. 2 that Bernstein conducted at Ely Cathedral, but since the film shows barely any interest in the craft of conducting, he may as well just be an elegant arm waver.
reviews.author: Bennett Campbell Ferguson

reviews.text: A fascinating, provocative, uplifting and sobering biopic, Maestro marks the second directorial venture of actor Bradley Cooper. Just like his debut feature, A Star is Born, the end result is a complete, must-see triumph.
reviews.author: Leigh Paatsch

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper’s Leonard Bernstein biopic is a stylish and intimate portrait of a complicated love story.
reviews.author: Joey Morona

reviews.text: Maestro is nothing short of magical, as Cooper’s direction leads to two of the best performances of 2023 in Cooper and Mulligan. It’s a cliché to say the two become their respective characters, yet this sentiment is entirely accurate here.
reviews.author: Matthew Creith

reviews.text: Leonard Bernstein's biopic is full of conviction and ideas, but also points to the problems of direction obsessed with making itself noticeable. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Alberto Corona

reviews.text: It’s a film full of creative swirls.
reviews.author: Moira MacDonald

reviews.text: Despite (or precisely because of that) having top producers and an artistic and commercial fabric designed for the Oscars, the film never quite reached me, much less fascinated or moved me. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Diego Batlle

reviews.text: The transitions between comedy and drama are inelegant and result in a certainly bipolar film when this is not what the film seems to want to say about its subject. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Fernando E. Juan Lima

reviews.text: Live performances of Bernstein’s compositions serve as the score to all this, and yet somehow Maestro never quite grasps the indefatigable love at the center of its subject’s life: music.
reviews.author: Andrew Marzoni

reviews.text:
Incredible, intimate, naturalistic, & cinematic experience.
Cooper transforms into an awe-inspiring performance that only blew me away. 
Mulligan is spectacular & brought me to tears
reviews.author: Zach Pope

reviews.text: A movie that is as exhilarating as it is unconventional, a fitting portrait of a man who was determined to always live life on his own terms, no matter the consequences.
reviews.author: Peter Howell

reviews.text: Bernstein's story just isn’t that engaging; his history simply isn’t that cinematic, exciting, surprising, or unconventional, considering that the bulk of his dramas are merely rows with his wife or quiet denials of gossipy subjects.
reviews.author: Mike Massie

reviews.text: While the performances - musical and otherwise - are top-notch, the script falls a little short.
reviews.author: Kip Mooney

reviews.text: If Cooper is the engine that makes the movie run and stay together, the top-billed Mulligan is the resilient soul that makes you fall in love with the world.
reviews.author: Dan Buffa

reviews.text: As the director, producer, co-writer and star, “Maestro” is Cooper’s world and we’re just living in it for 130 aesthetically pleasing minutes. He controls all that you will see and hear, nuances be damned.
reviews.author: Al Alexander

reviews.text: Directing and doing the best acting of his career, Cooper also showcases Carey Mulligan, passionate as the conductor’s long-suffering wife.
reviews.author: Richard Roeper

reviews.text: Good for Carey Mulligan & a the B&W parts, but overall this hits a flat note. By co-writing, directing and acting, Cooper is diminishing in all three categories, reducing a larger than life icon into a rather dry life. Lenny Bernstein, we hardly knew ye.
reviews.author: Patrick McDonald

reviews.text: There’s something superficial about [Cooper's] performance. Carey Mulligan, though, is astoundingly good as Lennie’s sainted, side-lined wife.
reviews.author: Paul Whitington

reviews.text: [Cooper] so comprehensively embodies Bernstein that he all but jumps off the screen during performances. It is thrilling to experience Cooper channeling such rapture throughout his and wife Felicia Montealegre’s tangled theatrical lives.
reviews.author: Diane Carson

reviews.text: From black and white to colour, breathless set-pieces to blazing rows, Maestro crams a lot into two hours. It's a little choppy in places and Cooper badly rushes the ending, but the film still manages to do justice to both its subjects.
reviews.author: Harry Guerin

reviews.text: Bernstein is played by Cooper with gusto, verve and wit. He races through a movie percolating with glamour, passion and sturm und drang, that form of romantic, emotional turmoil affecting mostly famous artists.
reviews.author: Tom Gliatto

reviews.text: Even though the film itself falters, Bernstein himself shines through, and maybe that’s its own kind of achievement.
reviews.author: Julia Glassman

reviews.text: I admired so many virtuosic moments without feeling an emotional connection to the material, and often found myself wondering who is sucking up all the oxygen in the room, Bernstein or the artist telling his story.
reviews.author: Radheyan Simonpillai

reviews.text: Director and co-writer Bradley Cooper leads a great cast in Maestro, but makes a common, biopic mistake in depicting the great artist.
reviews.author: James Verniere

reviews.text: An ouroboros of art and artist, a current creator channeling a historical one and wrestling with the same questions he faced, struggling in the same way to not let their passions subsume them, unsure whether they’re successful. It’s mesmerizing.
reviews.author: Joshua Rivera

reviews.text: an explosion of imaginaton, flying, sweeping, microscopic, macroscopic, outre cinematography, the interplay of black and white and colour, and the razor-sharp performances that withstand the power of the camera movements are born in radical exuberance.
reviews.author: Anne Brodie

reviews.text: What connects the real and the recreation is the unbridled sense of joy. As the cathedral vibrates with the voices soaring, the violinists bowing themselves into a frenzy, Cooper as Bernstein is in thrall — his hair a sweaty mess, the baton a blur.
reviews.author: Eli Glasner

reviews.text: Oh, frabjous film! Bradley Cooper’s astonishing high-wire act feels classic and modern at the same time: immersive and impressionistic, breathtakingly bold. A kick in the pants to mainstream cinema.
reviews.author: MaryAnn Johanson

reviews.text: Imitation and musical enthusiasm are all there is to this performance; in the dramatic scenes that make up the majority of “Maestro,” Cooper is the weak link that drags everything down.
reviews.author: Odie Henderson

reviews.text: Maestro strikes all the right notes and is masterfully orchestrated by Bradley Cooper who also gives a career best performance.
reviews.author: Daniel Baptista

reviews.text: Composer-conductor Leonard Bernstein is portrayed as a virtual force of nature in “Maestro,” and Bradley Cooper’s film aims to be one as well—for better and worse...a frequently frantic but sometimes solemn mosaic made up of bits and pieces of his life.
reviews.author: Frank Swietek

reviews.text: Everything in Maestro feels like a show, even—and especially—when it should not be.
reviews.author: Alan Zilberman

reviews.text: [Cooper and Singer] seem less interested in digging through the details than in capturing a mood, putting the audience in the whizzy headspace of a man constantly overflowing with creative energy and usually struggling to find the best ways to channel it.
reviews.author: David Sims

reviews.text: This is a big, juicy sort of film that inspires conversation about hair, makeup, prosthetics, lighting and cinematography. But no clear picture of Bernstein ever emerges. There is a self-consciousness about the filmmaking that keeps us at arm’s length.
reviews.author: Liz Braun

reviews.text: A stylish, passionate movie with just enough depth to both warm and break the heart.
reviews.author: Richard Crouse

reviews.text: Singing Mulligan’s praises is not enough. She deserves her own symphony.
reviews.author: Barry Hertz

reviews.text: Maestro is a movie of moments, all of which accrue into a vivid, if incomplete, whole.
reviews.author: Ann Hornaday

reviews.text: Maestro darts and hops around, bracingly; it’s a little like flipping through a big, stylish scrapbook, more or less but not strictly in chronological order.
reviews.author: Michael Phillips

reviews.text: Cooper throws himself into the role of Bernstein and delivers one of his finest performances, playing a complicated family man who desired men and couldn’t deny that desire even while loving his wife.
reviews.author: Randy Myers

reviews.text: Maestro is the closest thing to perfection I’ve seen on the screen in a very long time.
reviews.author: Rex Reed

reviews.text: Every shot is an art shot, so much that it almost seems to be screaming, "Look at me! Aren't you impressed? Give me an award!"
reviews.author: Tara McNamara

reviews.text: Cooper is directing big here, just as Bernstein always directed his orchestras big. It’s actually perfect for the material and captures the gusto of its subject.
reviews.author: Jeff York

reviews.text: Here’s a film that made me question what Cooper was trying to say about this man and his life. I say that in a good way, as it feels like a challenge laid before me that will be a benefit when reflecting on this film over time.
reviews.author: Aaron Neuwirth

reviews.text: The style of it is done with a dynamism that the story just doesn't have.
reviews.author: Amy Nicholson

reviews.text: While I enjoyed 'A Star is Born' much more, Bradley’s performance was superb in 'Maestro'. He’s still setting the bar high for himself as an artist. And it doesn’t hurt having your name and your film mentioned in awards conversations every now and then.
reviews.author: Jamie Broadnax

reviews.text: Cooper aims for the rafters, with lots of mile-a-minute banter, swooping camerawork, and perfectly synchronized stage business... but the spine of the movie is the glorious close-ups he gives his co-star.
reviews.author: Tom Shone

reviews.text: It is clear Bradley Cooper put his heart and soul into both his performance and his directing, and that is why this movie works as well as it does.
reviews.author: Tessa Smith

reviews.text: It’s exciting filmmaking, and Cooper rarely lets up.
reviews.author: Bill Goodykoontz

reviews.text: “Maestro” may be a loving tribute to Bernstein, but this disappointing film comes off as self-serving Oscar bait. At least the music is great.
reviews.author: Gary M. Kramer

reviews.text: It’s memorable, it’s sincere, it’s beautifully shot, the performances are outstanding, it leaves you on a high and it gives you some food for thought [...] a massive step forward for Bradley Cooper as a director!
reviews.author: Marianna Neal

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper's Maestro is a searingly intelligent drama...
reviews.author: Brian Viner

reviews.text: Maestro is an immaculate portrayal of two immensely complicated figures.
reviews.author: Jason Flatt

reviews.text: Watching Cooper and Mulligan portray their characters across decades, it’s hard not to be impressed, while nurturing a greater appreciation for why Cooper found Bernstein’s contributions and complications deserving of such a tribute.
reviews.author: Brian Lowry

reviews.text: Though the music is brilliantly handled, Carey Mulligan is the real heart and soul of what Cooper as director and co-writer (with Josh Singer) chooses to show.
reviews.author: David Nice

reviews.text: Maestro is Mulligan’s movie, and she is its roaring heart. The poise with which she holds sweetness, sacrifice, denial, love and rage within herself is exquisite.
reviews.author: Pippa Bailey

reviews.text: Maestro puts on an immersive show about a complex man who might always remain enigmatic in every sense of the word.
reviews.author: Alci Rengifo

reviews.text: Maestro’s excellence lies in being intelligent and bold but also, unashamedly, a movie.
reviews.author: Danny Leigh

reviews.text: It’s audaciously old-fashioned in its methods, and provides a swell answer to the question: Why the hell would I want to watch a movie about Leonard Bernstein when I could just watch West Side Story or Tar or whatever?
reviews.author: Nick Johnston

reviews.text: A capable biography of a queer artist, the woman who loved him and the music that moved them both, Maestro avoids many standard biopic tropes, but can’t quite escape the trappings of the genre.
reviews.author: Charles Lyons-Burt

reviews.text: In his sophomore feature, Bradley Cooper continues to blend music and film in a cinematic memory of the domestic life between Leonard Bernstein and Felicia Montealegre.
reviews.author: Jillian Chilingerian

reviews.text: There is a universe where Jake Gyllenhaal is starring as Leonard Bernstein in The American rather than Bradley Cooper in Maestro and I wish we could see that film.
reviews.author: Danielle Solzman

reviews.text: With its nonlinear structure, Maestro feels a little like a scrapbook of life moments – glittering career achievements; crackling explosions of domestic tension – and Cooper keeps up a zesty, kinetic energy throughout.
reviews.author: Wendy Ide

reviews.text: “Maestro” is anything but a failure. It's just an achievement that works a little too hard to be an Achievement.
reviews.author: Ty Burr

reviews.text: A virtuoso piece of filmmaking that tells a complicated, but ultimately moving love story.
reviews.author: Chris Bumbray

reviews.text: What "Maestro" wants us to know is that Bernstein was most fully alive, was most himself, when he was making music.
reviews.author: Chris Hewitt

reviews.text: A biopic that doesn’t play it by the book; this is suitably big, bold and messy, brimming with emotion and passion.
reviews.author: Andrew Gaudion

reviews.text: Cooper knows he has demonstrated spectacular skill, and he has effectively argued his thesis that Bernstein is a walking contradiction. But his conspicuous choices draw attention to themselves to sometimes disagreeable effect.
reviews.author: Brian Eggert

reviews.text: Cooper’s growth as a filmmaker is overshadowed by his and Mulligan’s performance which stand among the best of the year.
reviews.author: Dustin Chase

reviews.text: Cooper and Mulligan are effortless, but Maestro sidelines Bernstein’s music in favour of a solemn marriage piece.
reviews.author: Jack Hawkins

reviews.text: There is an irrefutable and intense stretch before, during, and after the movie’s apex that underlines every invested and brilliant measure of Cooper and his creative collaborators towards the goals of their intimate approach.
reviews.author: Don Shanahan

reviews.text: Makes a valiant effort to avoid the usual tropes of biographical dramas. Unfortunately, it leaves out the good parts, too.
reviews.author: Fred Topel

reviews.text: A soaring, beautifully crafted biopic about the talented, charismatic Bernstein & his relationship with wife Montealegre. Bradley Cooper is riveting & Carey Mulligan has never been better. One of the must-see films of the year. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Fico Cangiano

reviews.text: It is exquisitely inspiring. Kudos to Bradley Cooper for his commanding, demanding direction and research, plus his and Carey Mulligan’s passionate performances, bringing, this Maestro, more vibrant than ever, back to life.
reviews.author: Linda and Al Lerner

reviews.text: This bold and vibrant biopic is an affectionate tribute to the work and legacy of one of the greatest American composers, yet it doesn’t gloss over the hardships and personal struggles that shaped his artistic vision and creative process.
reviews.author: Todd Jorgenson

reviews.text: Maestro emerges as a bombastic aria of a biopic befitting its central subject.
reviews.author: Manuel Betancourt

reviews.text: It would take a more stringent script than the one Cooper’s written with Josh Singer to fully drain the sequences detailing Felicia’s illness of clichés, but he’s a good enough director to draw out a few genuine, tender emotions anyway...
reviews.author: Adam Nayman

reviews.text: Maestro goes down more easily if you accept the fact that it’s not a conventional biopic. It's an immersion in Bernstein’s emotionally charged life, his roving eye for bed partners, his bouts of depression, and his ferocity about music.
reviews.author: Robert Denerstein

reviews.text: Maestro holds its contradictions in balance; it sees the complexity and the tragedy of Lenny and Felicia’s romance, and also its undeniable tenderness and passion.
reviews.author: Justin Chang

reviews.text: Maestro is a fine portrait of a complicated marriage. But for a man who contained symphonies, that leaves a lot of notes unplayed.
reviews.author: Jake Coyle

reviews.text: Directed by Cooper, who also co-wrote the script with Josh Singer, the film serves up so much Sturm und Drang about the great man’s messed-up private life that it barely bothers to explore his creative genius.
reviews.author: Peter Rainer

reviews.text: A film that’s technically dazzling but emotionally frustrating.
reviews.author: Christy Lemire

reviews.text: Maestro hits all the right notes with stunning finesse.
reviews.author: Morgan Rojas

reviews.text: excepting Cooper’s willingness to cede the spotlight to his female costar, this is a very different film from “A Star Is Born,” both a biopic of a real person and riskier in its artistic choices, a marriage portrayed as mosaic.
reviews.author: Laura Clifford

reviews.text: Cooper’s sophomore film far outshines the common run of contemporary biopics in its artful construction and attention to emotional nuance.
reviews.author: Dana Stevens

reviews.text: More so-so than virtuoso.
reviews.author: Matt Singer

reviews.text: Cooper’s production is grand, bravura filmmaking.
reviews.author: Jonathan W. Hickman

reviews.text: The movie is not your typical biopic. It is more an examination of a man who lived two lives — one very public and flamboyant: the other, a more private and complex existence.
reviews.author: Bob Bloom

reviews.text: One of those biopics where the conflicts are all resolved with a half-hour to go, and then you have to just sit there waiting for everyone to die.
reviews.author: Sean Burns

reviews.text: Engrave an Oscar for Bradley Cooper for his heart-full-to-bursting tour de force as Leonard Bernstein. Alive with glorious music, the film resonates with the love the bisexual legend feels for the wife (a sublime Carey Mulligan) who lives with his demons.
reviews.author: Peter Travers

reviews.text: Bernstein feels flattened here, and thus the last few segments of the film–which ought to be the most impactful–provoke more comedic irony than empathy.
reviews.author: Ryan Silberstein

reviews.text: Mulligan and Cooper are too good for it not to be [enthralling]. Maybe it is all style and little substance, but its dual portrait (albeit shallow) is no less invigorating as a result.
reviews.author: Jared Mobarak

reviews.text: The film brims with energy from Bernstein's early years, cast in black and white, to the super color-saturated, drug-fueled 1980s. Its dazzling visuals match the music — and yes, somewhere in there, Maestro is also a movie about making music.
reviews.author: Anastasia Tsioulcas

reviews.text: It was a big juicy life, one that Cooper — who wrote the script with Josh Singer — has condensed into two eventful, visually expressive hours.
reviews.author: Manohla Dargis

reviews.text: It’s undeniable the commitment Cooper has made to Maestro and to bringing Bernstein’s story to the screen with complete authenticity.
reviews.author: Travis Hopson

reviews.text: Well-acted and occasionally potent, but often heavy-handed and shallow Oscar-bait.
reviews.author: Avi Offer

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper raises the baton with Maestro. The former Sexiest Man Alive is still a hunk, but he’s sobered up since The Hangover. He is a triple threat as writer/director/star for A Star is Born, but with Maestro, he’s triumphant.
reviews.author: T.J. Callahan

reviews.text: “Maestro” is gorgeously made, but much like “A Star Is Born,” the dramatic value of the picture often trails its incredible craftsmanship.
reviews.author: Brian Orndorf

reviews.text: For this Bernstein biopic, Bradley Cooper and company question how much beauty there really can be in the last word next to the flood of them that flows between the start and end. Stunningly rendered, with powerhouse work from Cooper and Carey Mulligan.
reviews.author: Nick Rogers

reviews.text: Maestro never truly gets under its subject’s skin, but it’s mightily impressive, full of brilliant filmmaking, many memorable scenes and a superb Carey Mulligan walking away with the entire movie.
reviews.author: Ian Freer

reviews.text: Maestro is worth watching for its transfixing performances and top-notch below-the-line craftsmanship. But it’s safe to say Bradley Cooper spent too much time in the Shallow while putting the narrative together
reviews.author: Robert Kojder

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper and Carey Mulligan deliver standout performances amidst innovative visuals and makeup; yet sluggish pacing and underdeveloped emotions hinder its full impact.
reviews.author: Jason Escamilla

reviews.text: The main problem with Maestro is how much it simplifies the man and this central relationship...
reviews.author: Mark Dujsik

reviews.text: It’s most appealing when it apes the rhythms of its subject’s work. Yet it also feels strangely distant from Bernstein as an artist, neglecting most details about his music.
reviews.author: Steve Erickson

reviews.text: As a biopic, Cooper elevates it to masterpiece level, worthy of the artistry of Leonard Bernstein. Maestro is a work of art.
reviews.author: Alan Ng

reviews.text: ‘Maestro’ is a deeply felt passion project that nourished me as few other recent pictures have and made me want to stand up and cheer. In other words, Bravo!
reviews.author: Leonard Maltin

reviews.text: “Maestro” exposes a truth about marriage that I always knew but could never quite articulate: To be truly known and understood can actually be scary.
reviews.author: Mick LaSalle

reviews.text: Cooper's musical-biopic magnum opus is a superbly crafted demonstration of his full confidence on both sides of the camera as it sprawls across the decades.
reviews.author: Neil Pond

reviews.text: I left feeling frustrated with how shallow and one-note the screenplay was.
reviews.author: Rachel Wagner

reviews.text: Director and star Bradley Cooper dazzlingly embodies the contradictory whole of conductor and West Side Story composer Leonard Bernstein...  And as his Costa Rica-born Broadway star wife, Felicia Montealegre, Carey Mulligan is even better.
reviews.author: Tim Appelo

reviews.text: Spurning a fruitless bid at comprehensiveness, Cooper has conjured something as restless and as headlong as his subject.
reviews.author: Anthony Lane

reviews.text: While this is ostensibly a portrait of one of the great artists of the 20th Century, its most fascinating note is its revelation of Bradley Cooper as a director who, like his subject, won’t settle for the ordinary.
reviews.author: Joanna Langfield

reviews.text: Cooper’s movie about composer Leonard Bernstein is brutal and brilliant.
reviews.author: Roger Friedman

reviews.text: Maestro is a visually stunning fever dream of a biopic that’s utterly chaotic, emotionally deficient, and regrettably hollow.
reviews.author: Jeff Nelson

reviews.text: A warts-and-all approach allows Bernstein feel human, a feat accomplished better here than in many films of its ilk.
reviews.author: Dan Scully

reviews.text: Sad elder-gay Lenny letting loose to Tears for Fears a pleasurable respite amid all the officially sanctioned bio-dreck.
reviews.author: Keith Uhlich

reviews.text: The shallow depth of etched glass is the extent to which Leonard Bernstein’s emotions are explored throughout this shameful film.
reviews.author: Maggie Lovitt

reviews.text: Cooper’s portrayal is nothing short of extraordinary; it’s the kind of career-best work that is undeniable. The cathedral scene, in particular, is a moment that will be talked about for years to come.
reviews.author: Mark Johnson

reviews.text: There are glimpses in this finely made film of someone much more interesting than we ever see here.
reviews.author: Rich Cline

reviews.text: the one place where Cooper could have delved a bit deeper was in the development of Bernstein's same-sex relationships, beyond the superficial. Certainly, the Bernstein family blessing was a factor, but it's a shame his gay life was given little nuance.
reviews.author: Frank J. Avella

reviews.text: Maestro's dynamic cinematic language speaks to the heart. The caliber of Bradley Cooper's direction is matched by a transformative performance as the great American composer opposite a dynamite Carey Mulligan as his actress-wife.
reviews.author: Hanna Flint

reviews.text: One can see just enough of Cooper in the film... such that Maestro isn’t a total wash, but he gets lost among the warring voices and sensibilities at play here, with most things about the production marred by a sense of uncertainty.
reviews.author: M.G. Mailloux

reviews.text: Maestro is a true work of cinematic beauty that honors the life and work of Lenard Berstein. Bradley Cooper’s role as lead actor and director showcased his deep commitment to the material and getting Berstein’s story as thoughtfully accurate as possible.
reviews.author: Emmanuel Noisette

reviews.text: Maestro is Cooper’s masterwork, elevating him both as a filmmaker and as an actor, to a new stratosphere.
reviews.author: Edward Douglas

reviews.text: Maestro is not a biopic of an artist so much as a human artwork, capturing the questions he provokes and the contradictory answers that define him.
reviews.author: Alexander Harrison

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper's Maestro is a harmonious, majestic, and tender symphony that beautifully captures an icon's legacy and the romance that enraptured his life.
reviews.author: David Gonzalez

reviews.text: What an empty, craven affront this movie is.
reviews.author: Jason Adams

reviews.text: All that Bradley Cooper wanted to capture is on the screen. The actor who clowned through the Hangover franchise and aptly directed A Star is Born has created a work of art.
reviews.author: Dwight Brown

reviews.text: Maestro does serve up a huge amount of movie in that it goes in rather hard on its attempt to be an artsy, prestige biopic with a capital ‘B’, and is subsequently a little uneven in its approach with pacing, humour, and storytelling.
reviews.author: Tori Brazier

reviews.text: There is never a shot wasted for your eyes or ears. It’s a rollercoaster of an experience and not just because of how high emotions are from beginning to end.
reviews.author: Emma Kiely

reviews.text: "Maestro" may present exhilarating moments of musical performances, but unlike the story's subject, it is a rather forgettable experience.
reviews.author: Rafael Motamayor

reviews.text: We don’t see a collection of the greatest hits when we reflect on our lives. Instead, we remember those specific memories of joy and suffering that made us feel the most alive. Bernstein wanted to share his life and his music with the world.
reviews.author: Sophia Ciminello

reviews.text:
Maestro is ambitious, intense, and poignant. It simultaneously weaves between heartwarming and heartbreaking. 

Bradley Cooper is now one of Hollywood’s best directors and is extraordinary as Leonard Bernstein. Carey Mulligan is equally great!
reviews.author: Sheraz Farooqi

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper embodies the great American composer, in a film that very much transcends its multiple pre-release controversies.
reviews.author: Stephen Silver

reviews.text: In this Leonard Bernstein biopic, his musical talent is a very secondary part of the story, compared to his personal relationships. Some viewers won't like the timeline jumping and small number of musical scenes, but the acting performances are stellar.
reviews.author: Carla Hay

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper’s sophomore feature ends up being unimpressive and uninspired, unlike the talents of the conductor being portrayed by this film’s director.
reviews.author: Hector A. Gonzalez

reviews.text: The viewer friendly film can be enjoyed even by viewers not familiar with the legendary conductor of the New York Philharmonic and his achievements as a composer.
reviews.author: Dennis Schwartz

reviews.text: Impeccably made with a true devotion to the subject matter, this rises above your standard award season biopic.
reviews.author: Kevin Carr

reviews.text: From the long takes that allow Bradley Cooper and Carey Mulligan to give two of the best performances of the year, to the brilliant, stylistic cinematography and unsurprisingly phenomenal score, Maestro is a masterpiece.
reviews.author: Lauren Bradshaw

reviews.text: With Maestro, Bradley Cooper has essentially reduced Leonard Bernstein’s boundary-pushing life and legacy to the sum total of its most accessible (read: audience-friendly) elements: his interpersonal relationships.
reviews.author: Kenji Fujishima

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper hits a soprano artistic note with a stunningly powerful biopic of American musical icon Leonard Bernstein. Carey Mulligan is damn good here. She is the actress to beat this award season.
reviews.author: Julian Roman

reviews.text: Maestro is creative and unusually well-organized for a biopic, all without overusing its narrative tools.  [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Ruben Peralta Rigaud

reviews.text: The good news is there’s no sophomore slump at play here. "A Star is Born" was no fluke and if anything, "Maestro" is more assured, a confident piece of work.
reviews.author: Charles Koplinski

reviews.text: Though it tells the story of iconic American composer and conductor Leonard Bernstein, Maestro's impressionistic style goes a long way to distinguish it from bog-standard biopics.
reviews.author: Christian Holub

reviews.text: A movie about a great artist and, considering how effectively it tells the story in an unconventional way, it is a work of art.
reviews.author: Jordan Hoffman

reviews.text: ...it’s hard not to feel like the whole thing is an awards grab circa the Kiss of the Spider Woman era, when filmmakers were still getting mainstream audiences used to the idea of queer characters in general.
reviews.author: Matthew Dougherty

reviews.text: We use genius and masterpiece too much, but this is a masterpiece about a true genius. With a chaotic touch, Bradley Cooper keeps this biopic moving like a great symphony.
reviews.author: EJ Moreno

reviews.text: Nothing Cooper does is organic or authentic, and his show-off performance is always stilted. He arduously thinks through every single choice — it’s time to scream into a pillow; cue the laugh; ready, set, cry.
reviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski

reviews.text: While Bradley Cooper takes some bold swings and conducts a visual symphony on screen, the result is rather superficial. Plus to completely ignore Leonard Bernstein's accomplishments, or those of his LGBT friends and colleagues, is an unfortunate choice.
reviews.author: Grace Randolph

reviews.text: Bernstein is in no way portrayed negatively, but deciding to make the romantic relationship the crux of Maestro has enabled the audience, towards the end, to become more emotionally invested in Montealegre than they are with Bernstein.
reviews.author: Cady Siregar

reviews.text: Maestro elegantly depicts the complexity and love of Leonard Bernstein via Bradley Cooper and Carey Mulligan.
reviews.author: Joey Magidson

reviews.text: Cooper could have played it safe with his sophomore feature, but instead he’s gone all out, utilising a number of ambitious directorial tricks and flourishes that lift this out of bog standard biopic territory, to frequently exhilarating effect.
reviews.author: Matthew Turner

reviews.text: There is so much to adore in Maestro, as Cooper’s supremely controlled vision touches greatness and sustains it.
reviews.author: Jonny Mahon-Heap

reviews.text: Even if I don't entirely love the film, this is easily some of the best cinematography in any film from 2023. Every last shot is perfectly composed, mirroring the perfectly conducted orchestras throughout Lenny's life.
reviews.author: Alex Billington

reviews.text: ...  A fond character study that luxuriates in its subject's livewire personality while acknowledging how exasperating and exhausting he could be.
reviews.author: Nicholas Barber

reviews.text: The tension between the private and the public becomes one of the driving forces of Maestro, which determinedly explores the life of a man caught between multiple contradictions. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Manu Yáñez

reviews.text: One of Maestro’s greatest strengths [is that] it’s highly rare in being an authorized dramatization of the life of an American legend—Bernstein’s children have approved of the film and attended the Venice premiere—that is admiring without being fawning.
reviews.author: Radhika Seth

reviews.text: [Maestro] didn’t grab me from the get-go but, powered by two compelling, charismatic lead performances, it did win me over in the emphatically emotional second half where all the high notes are hit.
reviews.author: Zhuo-Ning Su

reviews.text: The chemistry between Cooper and Mulligan is strong, whether they're sitting back to back in a park guessing the number their partner is thinking or when drama creeps in unexpectedly. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Pablo O. Scholz

reviews.text: [Bradley Cooper] turns this musician's biopic musician into an outrageous exhibition of himself at the hands of a melodrama that is essentially afraid of not disrespecting anyone. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Luis Martínez

reviews.text: Cooper shows us his subject’s mix of magnetism, volatility and childlike egotism but he remains a strangely elusive figure. It’s left to Mulligan’s Felicia to crack the film’s sometimes too-shiny facade and to give its story some bruising emotional depth.
reviews.author: Geoffrey Macnab

reviews.text: Cooper’s performance is sublime, delicately balancing the problem of playing a ham while not becoming a ham. He brings out Bernstein’s occasional cruelty and deep depression, which he tends to project on his wife.
reviews.author: John Bleasdale

reviews.text: It’s a film for cinephiles as well as musos and romantics, with its discrete ‘movements’ mirroring the movie making style of its time frame.
reviews.author: Philip De Semlyen

reviews.text: While those unfamiliar with Bernstein’s creative legacy might not fully comprehend the significance of his various artistic achievements, Cooper twirls this scenario into a rather captivating portrait of a marriage.
reviews.author: Nicholas Bell

reviews.text: The miracle of Maestro is that something works here; the actors invest, there is feeling and heart and style, which amply compensate for some of the more iffy touches and longueurs.
reviews.author: Caspar Salmon

reviews.text: If you are willing to embrace the film’s slower sensibilities, you’ll be rewarded with a careful portrait of a couple who redefine the scope of a successful marriage.
reviews.author: Anna McKibbin

reviews.text: Maestro is an enormous stylistic departure from Cooper's debut, the 2018 remake of A Star is Born. However, what they have in common (apart from depicting the love lives of artists) is that they’re both good films that come ever so close to being great.
reviews.author: Siddhant Adlakha

reviews.text: Moving, carefully crafted, and sometimes frustrating version of Bernstein’s booming highs and intimate lows. It's Cooper’s direction and Matthew Libatique’s cinematography that stand out most boldly.
reviews.author: Rory Doherty

reviews.text: Bradley Cooper’s Maestro puts the filmmaker front and center, but his acting far surpasses his directorial eye for his second feature.
reviews.author: Lex Briscuso

reviews.text: Cooper plays Leonard Bernstein as a man who belonged to everybody—and still does.
reviews.author: Stephanie Zacharek

reviews.text: Maestro exceeds expectations, certifying Bradley Cooper as a filmmaker with innate talent, just like Leonard Bernstein, who the former portrays brilliantly. Carey Mulligan joins the actor/director in the race for awards.
reviews.author: Manuel São Bento

reviews.text: [Bradley Cooper] certainly finds a savvy, timely angle to approach Bernstein’s story, with the attendant, large flaw that it actually writes its ostensible subject somewhat out of his own film.
reviews.author: David Katz

reviews.text: While Cooper’s film is traditional – it’s nowhere near as radical as Todd Field’s TÁR – it’s a bravura tribute to the creativity and artistry. You don’t need to be a student of Bernstein or his work to find this richly rewarding.
reviews.author: James Mottram

reviews.text: Cooper believes his portrayal of Felicia to be progressive but is regressive in adding the activist to the beaten trope of “the woman behind the man.”
reviews.author: Rafaela Sales Ross

reviews.text: Like Bernstein’s music, this movie won’t appeal to everybody, but it is an accomplished and moving biopic of two fascinating people, and a glimpse behind the public face of a truly great artist.
reviews.author: Jo-Ann Titmarsh

reviews.text: When we critics complain that studio pictures don’t take risks any more, Maestro is exactly the sort of film we wish they’d make instead. Not everything in it lands cleanly, but even its misses excite, and its direct hits are knockouts.
reviews.author: Robbie Collin

reviews.text: Maestro is honest about the larger-than-life flaws of its central character, and Cooper is impressive in the role.
reviews.author: Fionnuala Halligan

reviews.text: A stunning portrait of the artist as a charismatic narcissist in thrall to a marriage he believes in yet can’t completely live up to.
reviews.author: Owen Gleiberman

reviews.text: A soaring crescendo into sorrow.
reviews.author: David Rooney

reviews.text: This is a complex story of a man who can’t quite define the intersection of his art and personal life but seems to thrive on the ambiguity, a bigger than life and towering personality not at all sugar coated in this compelling take.
reviews.author: Pete Hammond

reviews.text: Behind its omissions, its contrivances, and Cooper’s straining for greatness that doesn’t always hit every note, “Maestro” is really Mulligan’s movie...
reviews.author: Ryan Lattanzio

reviews.text: This is not just a worthy tribute to one of the greatest figures in the American musical canon, but also one of the finest films of the year.
reviews.author: Marlow Stern

reviews.text: A nailed-on awards contender that distills the essence of a legend thanks to a pair of career-best performances. These little ducks are off to the races…
reviews.author: Jane Crowther

reviews.text: It’s only in an appreciation of Mulligan and Cooper’s full-bodied work that the greater whole finds resonance.
reviews.author: Richard Lawson

reviews.text: An astonishingly beautiful film, by turns heartbreaking, tragic and tender, one that is fully constructed around two incessantly committed career-high performances.
reviews.author: Kevin Maher

reviews.text: Sadly lacks Bernstein’s maverick spirit and warmth, or even captures anything about him you couldn’t glean from a quick skim read of Wikipedia.
reviews.author: Hannah Strong

reviews.text: A Star Is Born was wildly overpraised, but Maestro is the real deal: the rousing, complex and heartbreaking rhapsody its subject deserves.
reviews.author: Raphael Abraham

reviews.text: Maestro somehow proves that Cooper is a director of genuine vision, even though it’s not a particularly successful movie.
reviews.author: Bilge Ebiri

reviews.text: In the end, Cooper’s Maestro succeeds because it is candid about the sacrifices which art demands of its practitioners, and the sacrifices these practitioners demand of their families and partners.
reviews.author: Peter Bradshaw

reviews.text: “Maestro” does not go behind the music – it’s here to put on a show.
reviews.author: Ben Croll

reviews.text: For its occasional flaws, however, the net effect of Maestro is a powerful one.
reviews.author: Alonso Duralde

reviews.text: Cooper has continued to develop and improve his artistic eye... Maestro has moments of joy and greatness, it just fails to reach a crescendo deserving of the man, and the woman behind the great man.
reviews.author: Dallas King

reviews.text: Cooper hasn’t escaped all of the limitations of the subgenre, but at least this shows his passion for storytelling can still be arresting no matter where he stands by the camera.
reviews.author: Josh Parham

reviews.text: Mulligan’s distinctive trait of vulnerability-as-composure matches the rascal energy of Cooper’s Lenny most of the time, but even if the chemistry is not always right, they meet perfectly in acts of affection and in fights.
reviews.author: Savina Petkova

synopsis: Maestro is a towering and fearless love story chronicling the lifelong relationship between Leonard Bernstein and Felicia Montealegre Cohn Bernstein. A love letter to life and art, Maestro at its core is an emotionally epic portrayal of family and love.
